name: Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges
description: A review paper critically examining the current state of Visual Question Answering (VQA) in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets (DAQUAR, COCO-QA, The VQA Dataset, FM-IQA, Visual7W, Visual Genome, SHAPES), evaluation metrics, and algorithms. The paper discusses limitations of current datasets with regard to their ability to properly train and assess VQA algorithms, exhaustively reviews existing algorithms for VQA, and discusses possible future directions for VQA and image understanding research.
creator: Kushal Kafle and Christopher Kanan, Chester F. Carlson Center for Imaging Science, Rochester Institute of Technology
citeAs: Kafle, K. and Kanan, C. (2017). Visual Question Answering: Datasets, Algorithms, and Future Challenges. arXiv:1610.01465v4 [cs.CV].
rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets are reviewed. Data collection methods vary by dataset: DAQUAR uses images from NYU-DepthV2 with manually and automatically generated QA pairs; COCO-QA uses an NLP algorithm to automatically derive QA pairs from COCO image captions; The VQA Dataset (COCO-VQA) employed Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions and answers for COCO images; FM-IQA collected human-generated questions and answers originally in Chinese with English translations; Visual Genome used crowdsourced dense image annotations with both free-form and region-specific question prompting; Visual7W is a subset of Visual Genome; SHAPES consists of programmatically generated questions about synthetic shape images.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data, Software Collection, Others
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The English version of the FM-IQA dataset was unavailable from the provided download link at the time of the review.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images sourced from: NYU-DepthV2 Dataset (DAQUAR), Microsoft COCO dataset with 328,000 images (COCO-QA, COCO-VQA, FM-IQA, Visual7W), YFCC100M and COCO images (Visual Genome), synthetic cartoon images (SYNTH-VQA), and programmatically generated shape images (SHAPES). QA pairs were generated either manually by human annotators (via Amazon Mechanical Turk for COCO-VQA), automatically via NLP algorithms (COCO-QA), or through crowdsourcing (Visual Genome).
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Datasets released beginning in 2014 through the time of the article (2017). DAQUAR was the first major VQA dataset released in 2014.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For COCO-QA, an NLP algorithm derived QA pairs from COCO image captions by transforming captions into questions (e.g., 'A boy is playing Frisbee' becomes 'What is the boy playing?' with answer 'frisbee'). For SYNTH-VQA, synthetic scenes were constructed from over 100 objects, 30 animal models, and 20 human cartoon models with deformable limbs and facial expressions. For Visual Genome, region-specific question prompting was used alongside free-form questions to reduce bias. The Yin and Yang dataset was built on top of SYNTH-VQA to eliminate answer biases by creating paired images where the same question has different correct answers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For COCO-QA, longer sentences were broken into smaller chunks for NLP processing to generate QA pairs, though this caused grammatical errors in some cases. For COCO-VQA multiple-choice format, 18 answer choices were constructed including: the correct answer (most frequent from 10 annotators), 3 plausible answers (collected without seeing the image), top 10 most popular answers in the dataset, and randomly selected correct answers for other questions. For Visual7W multiple-choice, plausible answers were collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation protocols varied by dataset: DAQUAR used a combination of manual and automatic annotation with an average of 3 ground truth answers per question; COCO-QA used automatic NLP-based generation from captions; COCO-VQA employed Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers who were asked to 'Stump a smart robot' to generate questions, with a separate pool of workers generating answers, resulting in 10 independent answers per question; FM-IQA used human-generated questions and answers; Visual Genome used two modes - free-form annotation and region-specific annotation prompted by bounding-box regions; Visual7W used annotations sourced from Visual Genome with multiple-choice options collected by having annotators answer without seeing the image.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) was used for COCO-VQA annotation. Crowdsourcing platforms were used for Visual Genome.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is approximately 83.3% using the AccuracyVQA metric. For 'Why' questions, over 59% have fewer than three annotators giving exactly the same answer, making it impossible to achieve full score. More than 13% of yes/no questions in COCO-VQA have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. The consensus-based evaluation metric for COCO-VQA awards full score if the algorithm agrees with 3 or more of the 10 annotators. DAQUAR-consensus collected an average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question and proposed average consensus and min consensus evaluation approaches. Annotator disagreement was found even for simple questions, with some answers being complete antonyms (e.g., left and right).
rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question, 3 questions per image; DAQUAR: average of 3 ground truth answers per question (DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5); Visual Genome: average of 17 QA pairs per image; SYNTH-VQA: 3 questions per scene, 10 ground truth answers per question; COCO-QA: 4 question types, single word answers.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: NLP algorithm used to automatically generate QA pairs from COCO captions for COCO-QA dataset. Edge Boxes used for bounding box region proposals in some VQA algorithms. word2vec used for computing similarity between words in questions and object labels.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: SYNTH-VQA synthetic human models span different age, gender, and races to provide variation in appearance. No other personal or sensitive information about real individuals is explicitly collected.
rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA has potential applications as an aid to blind and visually impaired individuals, enabling them to get information about images on the web and in the real world. VQA could improve human-computer interaction as a natural way to query visual content and could be used for image retrieval without using image meta-data or tags. A robust VQA system is considered a component of a Turing Test for image understanding.
rai:dataBiases: Multiple forms of bias are identified across datasets: (1) Language bias - question-only models achieve up to 49.6% accuracy on COCO-VQA without using images; (2) Answer distribution bias - 'yes/no' answers span about 38% of COCO-VQA questions, with 59% answered 'yes'; answering 'yes' to all yes/no questions yields 71% accuracy using AccuracyVQA instead of the expected ~50%; (3) Question type bias - questions beginning with 'Is there' can be answered 'yes' with 85.2% accuracy; (4) DAQUAR contains exclusively indoor scenes limiting question variety; (5) COCO-QA only has four question types limited to COCO caption content; (6) Visual Genome's free-form questions tend toward similar holistic content questions; (7) Natural image datasets have contextual biases (e.g., street scenes more likely to have dogs than zebras); (8) VQA systems are sensitive to question phrasing, with MCB-ensemble achieving 33.6% vs 86.4% accuracy on the same task depending on question wording; (9) Attentive mechanisms may attend to biased regions rather than task-relevant regions.
rai:dataLimitations: DAQUAR is too small to train complex models and contains only indoor scenes with cluttered images and extreme lighting; humans achieve only 50.2% accuracy. COCO-QA has grammatical errors and nonsensical questions due to NLP generation flaws, only four question types, and single-word answers with only 435 unique answers. COCO-VQA contains subjective opinion-seeking questions without single objective answers, questions answerable without the image due to language bias, and inter-human agreement of only 83.3%. FM-IQA requires human judges for evaluation making it impractical for iterative development. Visual Genome's long-tailed answer distribution makes open-ended evaluation challenging, and answer diversity may artificially stem from phrasing variations. Multiple-choice evaluation allows systems to exploit answer biases rather than truly solving VQA. Current datasets are insufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has 'solved' VQA. All datasets use evaluation metrics that treat every question with equal weight, disadvantaging rare but complex question types.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation of VQA algorithms. Benchmarking visual question answering systems. Evaluating image understanding capabilities as a component of a Visual Turing Test. Applications include: aiding blind and visually impaired individuals, improving human-computer interaction for querying visual content, and image retrieval without metadata. The paper recommends mean per-question-type performance as a more meaningful evaluation metric than overall accuracy.
